summary: Looks at how attacks on common hash functions affect Cryptographically Generated Addresses and updates the CGA specification to support multiple hash algorithms. This lets implementations move away from a weakened hash. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: If the tool that makes a fingerprint for an address gets weak, this lets you switch to a stronger one.

questions: what is a cryptographically generated address
what is the cga sec field
does sha-1 collision attack affect cgas
how do cgas support multiple hash algorithms
subtitle: Why SHA-1 attacks do not break CGAs, and how the Sec bits can signal other hash algorithms later.

tldr.problem: Cryptographically Generated Addresses are hard coded to SHA-1, and recent attacks on common hash functions raised the question of whether CGAs are safe and how they could move to another hash.
tldr.mechanism: The memo concludes current CGA uses are not affected, then uses the 3-bit Sec field of an address to select the hash algorithm. It creates an IANA registry, CGA SEC, whose entries point to the RFC defining the generation procedure.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3972 is updated so CGAs can migrate to a stronger hash without a major disruption. Only three SHA-1 based Sec values are defined; no other hash is picked.

today: RFC 4982 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 3972, and the unit metadata shows nothing has obsoleted or updated it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Recent attacks on commonly used hash functions worried the Internet community. The recommended approach is to analyze the effect on each protocol that uses hashes, and to make sure those protocols can move to a more secure hash without major disruption.

This document does that analysis for Cryptographically Generated Addresses (CGAs) from RFC 3972. It reaches two conclusions. First, the security of protocols that use CGAs is not affected by the available attacks. Second, the hash function is hard coded in the CGA specification. The memo therefore updates RFC 3972 to allow alternative hash functions and creates a new IANA registry for the hash algorithms used in CGAs.
sections.eli5: People found tricks against some fingerprint recipes. This memo checks whether special addresses are in danger and prepares a way to swap recipes.

sections.title: Impact of Collision Attacks on CGAs
sections.content:
Recent attacks weaken the collision-free property of certain hash functions, including SHA-1, which CGAs use. An attacker can find two messages with the same hash value with far fewer than 2^(L/2) attempts. These attacks mostly threaten non-repudiation, where one party could present either of two messages interchangeably after one was signed. Both messages must come from the same party.

Current CGA uses do not provide non-repudiation. They prove ownership of an address and bind it to alternative addresses. The RFC lists three:

  • Protecting the shim6 protocol, where the list of alternative addresses is signed with the CGA private key.
  • Securing Mobile IPv6 (RFC 3775), where the Binding Update carrying the care-of address is signed.
  • Secure Neighbor Discovery (RFC 3971), where the layer 2 address information is signed.

All of these protect a conversation between two peers from third parties, not from the peer itself. A weaker collision resistance therefore enables no additional attack.
sections.eli5: The trick only helps someone who makes both of two fake notes themselves. These addresses guard against outsiders, so the trick does not help.

sections.title: Why Support Multiple Hashes Anyway
sections.content:
CGAs as defined in RFC 3972 are bound to SHA-1 and nothing else. Even though no new vulnerability appears in current uses, the memo calls it wise to allow other hash functions, for two reasons.

First, future applications of CGAs may be vulnerable to collision attacks on SHA-1, and alternative hashes would let those applications use CGAs. Second, one lesson of the recent attacks is that other properties of common hash functions may someday be broken, so protocols should make such a transition as easy as possible.
sections.eli5: Even though nothing is broken today, it is smart to keep a spare recipe ready in case the current one goes bad later.

sections.title: Where to Encode the Hash Function
sections.content:
The memo weighs where to record which hash was used. Putting it in an extension to the CGA Parameter Data Structure is open to bidding down (downgrade) attacks: an attacker could find a parameter structure naming a weaker hash that produces the same address value, so the strong hash adds no protection. The conclusion is that the hash function must be encoded in the address itself, using likely 2 or 3 bits.

  • Taking more bits from the hash bits of the interface identifier weakens the CGA and cannot be backward compatible.
  • Using the u and g bits is not a good idea because they have kept their original purpose in all interface identifier generation mechanisms.
  • The chosen option is the Sec bits. They add difficulty to CGA generation as protection against brute force, and the proposal is to make them also select the hash function.

For example, Sec value 000 would mean SHA-1 with 0 bits of hash2 required to be zero, and 001 would mean SHA-1 with 16 bits of hash2 required to be zero. Other values could name alternative hashes, but the memo defines no concrete hash for them.
sections.eli5: The note saying which recipe was used has to be part of the address, not a separate paper someone could swap. A few spare bits in the address do that job.

sections.title: Generation Procedure and Reusing Sec Values
sections.content:
A new IANA registry, SEC, has an entry per Sec value. Each entry points to an RFC that defines the CGA generation procedure that MUST be used for that value. That procedure may change more than the hash. For example, a longer Modifier may be needed if the number of zeros required in hash2 exceeds the currently defined bound of 112 bits. The defining RFC MUST also state the minimum acceptable key length for that Sec value, so hash and public key protection stay balanced.

Since there are only 8 Sec values, reusing one may eventually be necessary, but only as a last resort and after a long gap, because old and new implementations would read the value differently and fail to interoperate. In the worst case verification fails and both nodes fall back to unprotected IPv6 addresses. An implementation must not support two meanings of a Sec value at once.
sections.eli5: Each setting points to a rulebook that says how to build the address. Reusing an old setting is risky, because old and new devices would read it differently.

sections.title: The CGA SEC Registry
sections.content:
The memo defines a registry called CGA SEC for the Sec field from RFC 3972. Values are 3-bit unsigned integers, and future assignments need Standards Action. Each assignment has a name, a value and the RFC number defining the generation procedure.

Three initial values are assigned: SHA-1_0hash2bits (000), SHA-1_16hash2bits (001) and SHA-1_32hash2bits (010), each referencing RFC 3972 and RFC 4982. The Security Considerations section says only that the document is about security issues and protection against potential attacks on hash functions.
sections.eli5: A public list records each setting, its number, and the rulebook it follows. Three settings are listed so far.
